# Task 4: Building a Greenlight Risk Model

## Data Preparation

```{r}
#| label: task1-setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

focus_genres <- c(
  "Action", "Comedy", "Drama",
  "Horror", "Animation"
)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year),
         release_year <= 2016) |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget < 10000, NA_real_, 
                     as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue <= 0, NA_real_,
                      as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = if_else(
      !is.na(budget) & !is.na(revenue),
      revenue / budget,
      NA_real_
    ),
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )

movies_focus <- movies_clean |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% focus_genres)
```

## Outcome and Predictor Definitions

```{r}
#| label: task4-outcome
#| include: false

# movies_clean was created in the shared setup chunk.

task4_data <- movies_clean |>
  mutate(
    flop = case_when(
      is.na(roi) ~ NA_integer_,
      roi < 1 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L      
    )
  )

# Check the outcome categories.
task4_data |>
  count(flop, name = "number_of_films")
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-data-checks
#| include: false

# Check missing values in the selected predictors.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    missing_genre = sum(is.na(primary_genre)),
    missing_franchise = sum(is.na(franchise_status)),
    missing_budget = sum(is.na(budget_m)),
    missing_crew = sum(is.na(crew_size))
  )

# Count films with complete information for modelling.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    complete_model_cases = sum(
      complete.cases(
        flop,
        primary_genre,
        franchise_status,
        budget_m,
        crew_size
      )
    )
  )
```

Financial risk was assessed using return on investment (ROI), calculated as box-office revenue divided by production budget. A film was classified as a *flop* when its ROI was below 1, indicating that reported revenue did not recover the production budget. Films with an ROI of 1 or higher were classified as *non-flops*, while those with missing ROI were left unclassified.

Of the 4,801 films examined, 785 were identified as flops and 2,429 as non-flops, with the remaining 1,587 lacking sufficient financial information for classification. Among the 3,214 films with known outcomes, the observed flop rate was approximately 24.4%.

Logistic regression was selected because the outcome is binary, allowing the model to estimate the probability of a film flopping while keeping predicted values between 0 and 1. Linear regression is less appropriate because its predictions are not restricted to this range, whereas Poisson regression is primarily designed for count outcomes rather than binary classifications.

The proposed predictors were primary genre, franchise status, production budget and crew size, as these characteristics can reasonably be considered before a film receives production approval. After accounting for missing outcome and predictor information, 3,213 films had complete observations available for modelling. However, the substantial amount of missing financial data remains an important limitation, as films with recorded outcomes may not be representative of the wider dataset, potentially introducing selection bias.

## Frequentist Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-initial-model
#| include: false

task4_initial_model <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_m + crew_size,
  data = task4_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_initial_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-genre-diagnostic
#| include: false

task4_data |>
  filter(!is.na(flop), !is.na(primary_genre)) |>
  count(primary_genre, flop) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = flop,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "flop_"
  ) |>
  mutate(total = flop_0 + flop_1) |>
  arrange(total)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-data
#| include: false

task4_model_data <- task4_data |>
  mutate(
    budget_10m = budget_m / 10,
    crew_10 = crew_size / 10
  ) |>
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      flop,
      primary_genre,
      franchise_status,
      budget_10m,
      crew_10
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-model
#| include: false

task4_frequentist <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_10m + crew_10,
  data = task4_model_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_frequentist)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-odds
#| include: false

odds_ratios <- exp(coef(task4_frequentist))

wald_intervals <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

task4_odds_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(odds_ratios),
  Odds_Ratio = odds_ratios,
  CI_Lower = exp(wald_intervals[, 1]),
  CI_Upper = exp(wald_intervals[, 2])
)

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  print(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-results
#| echo: false

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Predictor %in% c(
      "franchise_statusFranchise",
      "budget_10m",
      "crew_10"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(
      Predictor,
      franchise_statusFranchise = "Franchise (vs original)",
      budget_10m = "Budget (+$10 million)",
      crew_10 = "Crew (+10 members)"
    ),
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor",
      "Odds ratio",
      "95% CI lower",
      "95% CI upper"
    ),
    caption = "Selected frequentist logistic regression results"
  )
```
**Interpretation**

The frequentist logistic regression was fitted using 3,213 films with complete information. After accounting for genre, budget and crew size, franchise films had approximately 77.6% lower odds of flopping than original films (OR = 0.224, 95% CI: 0.126–0.399). A further $10 million in budget was associated with 4.0% lower odds of flopping (OR = 0.960, 95% CI: 0.936–0.985), while an additional 10 crew members was associated with 9.4% lower odds (OR = 0.906, 95% CI: 0.877–0.936). These findings suggest that franchise status, budget and crew size are associated with financial outcomes, although they do not establish causal relationships.

**Limitations**

The model has two important limitations. First, the Foreign genre contained only one film with a known outcome, which was a flop. This resulted in complete separation and an unstable coefficient, making its estimated odds ratio unreliable. Second, the analysis used 3,213 of the original 4,801 films because observations with missing information were excluded. If missing financial data are not random, the estimated relationships may not represent all films. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results and comparing them with the Bayesian model.

## Bayesian Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-data-checks
#| include: false

# Outcome balance
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::count(flop) |>
  dplyr::mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))

# Number of flops and non-flops in each genre
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::group_by(primary_genre) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    films = dplyr::n(),
    flops = sum(flop == 1),
    non_flops = sum(flop == 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(films)

# Predictor scales
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    budget_sd = sd(budget_10m),
    crew_sd = sd(crew_10),
    budget_median = median(budget_10m),
    crew_median = median(crew_10),
    budget_max = max(budget_10m),
    crew_max = max(crew_10)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-predictors
#| include: false

task4_budget_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$budget_10m)
task4_budget_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$budget_10m)

task4_crew_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$crew_10)
task4_crew_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$crew_10)

task4_bayesian_data <- task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    budget_z = (budget_10m - task4_budget_mean) /
      task4_budget_sd,
    crew_z = (crew_10 - task4_crew_mean) /
      task4_crew_sd
  )

summary(task4_bayesian_data[, c("budget_z", "crew_z")])
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-check
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

# Draw hypothetical coefficients from proposed priors
prior_intercept <- 2.5 * rt(10000, df = 3)
prior_franchise <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
prior_budget <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
prior_crew <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)

# Illustrative profile: original film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_original <- plogis(prior_intercept)

# Illustrative profile: franchise film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_franchise <- plogis(
  prior_intercept + prior_franchise
)

# Summarise implied prior probabilities
rbind(
  Original = quantile(
    prior_prob_original,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  ),
  Franchise = quantile(
    prior_prob_franchise,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-comparison
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

n_draws <- 10000

# Candidate intercept priors
intercept_a <- 2.5 * rt(n_draws, df = 3)
intercept_b <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = -1, sd = 1)

# Other coefficient priors
franchise_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 1.5)
budget_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)
crew_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)

# Representative profiles on standardised scales
prior_profiles <- data.frame(
  profile = c(
    "Original, average scale",
    "Franchise, average scale",
    "Original, higher scale"
  ),
  franchise = c(0, 1, 0),
  budget_z = c(0, 0, 1),
  crew_z = c(0, 0, 1)
)

# Function to summarise implied probabilities
check_prior <- function(intercept, prior_name) {

  results <- lapply(
    seq_len(nrow(prior_profiles)),
    function(i) {

      log_odds <- intercept +
        franchise_effect * prior_profiles$franchise[i] +
        budget_effect * prior_profiles$budget_z[i] +
        crew_effect * prior_profiles$crew_z[i]

      probabilities <- plogis(log_odds)

      data.frame(
        prior = prior_name,
        profile = prior_profiles$profile[i],
        lower = quantile(probabilities, 0.025),
        median = median(probabilities),
        upper = quantile(probabilities, 0.975)
      )
    }
  )

  dplyr::bind_rows(results)
}

prior_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  check_prior(intercept_a, "A: Student-t(3, 0, 2.5)"),
  check_prior(intercept_b, "B: Normal(-1, 1)")
)

print(prior_comparison)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-final-priors
#| include: false

# Design matrix for Bayesian logistic regression
task4_formula <- flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status +
  budget_z + crew_z

task4_X <- model.matrix(
  task4_formula,
  data = task4_bayesian_data
)

task4_y <- task4_bayesian_data$flop

# Prior standard deviations for regression coefficients
task4_prior_sd <- rep(1.5, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_sd) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_sd["(Intercept)"] <- 1
task4_prior_sd["budget_z"] <- 0.5
task4_prior_sd["crew_z"] <- 0.5

# Prior means
task4_prior_mean <- rep(0, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_mean) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_mean["(Intercept)"] <- -1

# Log-posterior = log-likelihood + log-prior
task4_log_posterior <- function(beta) {

  eta <- drop(task4_X %*% beta)

  # Numerically stable Bernoulli log-likelihood
  log_likelihood <- sum(
    task4_y * eta -
      (pmax(eta, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(eta))))
  )

  log_prior <- sum(
    dnorm(
      beta,
      mean = task4_prior_mean,
      sd = task4_prior_sd,
      log = TRUE
    )
  )

  log_likelihood + log_prior
}
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-predictive
#| include: false

task4_prior_fit <- brms::brm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status +
    budget_z + crew_z,
  data = task4_bayesian_data,
  family = brms::bernoulli(),
  prior = task4_bayesian_priors,
  sample_prior = "only",
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  chains = 2,
  iter = 1000,
  warmup = 500,
  cores = 2,
  seed = 2420,
  file = "task4_prior_predictive_fit"
)

# Prior-predictive probabilities for all modelled films
prior_probabilities <- brms::posterior_epred(
  task4_prior_fit
)

# Distribution of the average implied flop probability
prior_average_risk <- rowMeans(prior_probabilities)

quantile(
  prior_average_risk,
  c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
)

# Simulated number of flops in the modelling sample
prior_simulated_outcomes <- brms::posterior_predict(
  task4_prior_fit
)

prior_flop_counts <- rowSums(prior_simulated_outcomes)

quantile(
  prior_flop_counts,
  c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-fit
#| include: false

# Locate a suitable starting point for Metropolis sampling
task4_mode <- optim(
  par = task4_prior_mean,
  fn = function(beta) -task4_log_posterior(beta),
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000)
)

print(task4_mode$convergence)

# Estimate the proposal covariance
task4_proposal_cov <- solve(task4_mode$hessian)

# Short pilot run to assess the sampler
set.seed(2420)

task4_mh_pilot <- MCMCpack::MCMCmetrop1R(
  fun = task4_log_posterior,
  theta.init = as.numeric(task4_mode$par),
  V = task4_proposal_cov,
  tune = 0.8,
  burnin = 1000,
  mcmc = 3000,
  thin = 1,
  logfun = TRUE,
  verbose = 0
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-diagnostics
#| include: false

# Pilot acceptance and rejection rates
task4_pilot_rejection <- coda::rejectionRate(
  task4_mh_pilot
)

task4_pilot_acceptance <- 1 - task4_pilot_rejection

cat(
  "Pilot rejection rate:",
  round(task4_pilot_rejection, 3),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Pilot acceptance rate:",
  round(task4_pilot_acceptance, 3),
  "\n"
)

# Effective sample size for each coefficient
task4_pilot_ess <- coda::effectiveSize(
  task4_mh_pilot
)

cat(
  "Minimum pilot ESS:",
  round(min(task4_pilot_ess), 1),
  "\n"
)
```


*Bayesian model and prior justification*

A Bayesian logistic regression was fitted to the same 3,213 films used in the frequentist analysis. The model included primary genre, franchise status, budget and crew size. Budget and crew size were standardised to make the prior assumptions easier to interpret. Posterior distributions were estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), implemented through Stan's No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS).

Weakly informative Normal priors were assigned to the log-odds coefficients: Normal(0, 1.5) for genre and franchise effects and Normal(0, 0.5) for standardised budget and crew size. An initial broad intercept prior was examined before selecting Normal(-1, 1). Prior-predictive checks indicated that the revised specification allowed substantial variation in flop risk without concentrating almost all probability on extreme outcomes.

*Bayesian findings and limitations*

The model showed satisfactory sampling diagnostics, with R-hat values of approximately 1.00, adequate effective sample sizes and no divergent transitions. Franchise status, higher budgets and larger crews were associated with lower flop odds.

The Foreign genre remained highly uncertain. Its posterior log-odds coefficient was 0.88, with a 95% credible interval of −1.57 to 3.43. Since only one Foreign film had a known outcome, the prior helped regularise the estimate but could not compensate for the lack of data. These findings describe associations rather than causal effects.

## Model Comparison

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-comparison-data
#| include: false

# Frequentist estimates and 95% confidence intervals
frequentist_coefs <- coef(task4_frequentist)
frequentist_ci <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

# Bayesian posterior summaries
bayesian_coefs <- brms::fixef(task4_bayesian)

# Compare coefficients on matching scales
comparison <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Franchise", "Budget (+$10m)", "Crew (+10)"),
  Frequentist_OR = exp(frequentist_coefs[
    c("franchise_statusFranchise", "budget_10m", "crew_10")
  ]),
  Frequentist_Lower = exp(frequentist_ci[
    c("franchise_statusFranchise", "budget_10m", "crew_10"), 1
  ]),
  Frequentist_Upper = exp(frequentist_ci[
    c("franchise_statusFranchise", "budget_10m", "crew_10"), 2
  ]),
  Bayesian_OR = exp(c(
    bayesian_coefs["franchise_statusFranchise", "Estimate"],
    bayesian_coefs["budget_z", "Estimate"] / task4_budget_sd,
    bayesian_coefs["crew_z", "Estimate"] / task4_crew_sd
  )),
  Bayesian_Lower = exp(c(
    bayesian_coefs["franchise_statusFranchise", "Q2.5"],
    bayesian_coefs["budget_z", "Q2.5"] / task4_budget_sd,
    bayesian_coefs["crew_z", "Q2.5"] / task4_crew_sd
  )),
  Bayesian_Upper = exp(c(
    bayesian_coefs["franchise_statusFranchise", "Q97.5"],
    bayesian_coefs["budget_z", "Q97.5"] / task4_budget_sd,
    bayesian_coefs["crew_z", "Q97.5"] / task4_crew_sd
  ))
)

print(comparison)
```


```{r}
#| label: task4-posterior-probability
#| include: false

task4_posterior_draws <- brms::as_draws_df(task4_bayesian)

franchise_draws <- task4_posterior_draws[["b_franchise_statusFranchise"]]

prob_franchise_negative <- mean(franchise_draws < 0)

print(prob_franchise_negative)
```

The frequentist and Bayesian models produced closely aligned results. For franchise films, the frequentist odds ratio was 0.224 (95% confidence interval: 0.126–0.399), compared with a Bayesian odds ratio of 0.229 (95% credible interval: 0.127–0.388). Budget and crew size also showed similar negative associations with flop odds across both models.

Although the intervals are numerically similar, their interpretations differ. A frequentist 95% confidence interval refers to the long-run coverage of the estimation procedure, whereas a Bayesian 95% credible interval contains 95% of the posterior probability for the parameter, conditional on the model and priors.

All 4,000 sampled posterior draws for the franchise coefficient were negative, giving an estimated posterior probability above 99.9% that franchise status is associated with lower flop odds, after accounting for genre, budget and crew size. The agreement between the models strengthens confidence in the direction of these associations, although neither approach establishes causation.
